actions.justification: Mandatory first step — continuous monitoring of HR, BP, SpO2, RR to evaluate hemodynamic stability and guide urgency of further workup in this pregnant patient with suspected PE.
Mandatory — Wells score for PE stratifies pre-test probability in this patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, guiding the diagnostic pathway (D-dimer vs. direct imaging).
Mandatory — D-dimer is a key initial diagnostic test for PE; if low pre-test probability, a negative D-dimer can rule out PE and avoid radiation exposure in this pregnant patient.

12-lead ECG is a Class I recommendation for acute chest pain to evaluate for STEMI and ST changes within 10 minutes of first medical contact. Patient presents with pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea, making ECG essential for initial workup.

Patient is pregnant with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, likely PE given Wells score assessment already completed. Supplemental oxygen is appropriate supportive care during initial assessment even with SpO2 98% given the clinical context of suspected PE in pregnancy.

Suspected pulmonary embolism in a pregnant patient warrants early pulmonology consultation to guide diagnostic imaging decisions (CTPA vs V/Q scan) and management, given the complexity of anticoagulation in pregnancy.

Chest X-ray is indicated as part of initial workup for acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain to evaluate for alternative diagnoses (pneumothorax, pneumonia, pleural effusion) and is a standard component of PE workup per chest pain guidelines.

CT pulmonary angiography is the definitive imaging modality for diagnosing pulmonary embolism. With acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and pregnancy (a major risk factor for VTE), CT-PA is indicated after Wells score assessment to confirm or exclude PE.
Echocardiogram can assess for right ventricular strain or dysfunction, which would indicate hemodynamic significance of a suspected PE and guide urgency of anticoagulation or escalation of therapy.

ECG should be obtained to evaluate for right heart strain pattern (S1Q3T3), sinus tachycardia, or other changes consistent with PE in this pregnant patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Note: order_ecg was already done but order_imaging_ecg is a distinct available action ID.

Lower extremity Doppler ultrasound is indicated to evaluate for DVT, which would support the diagnosis of PE in this pregnant patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Safe in pregnancy (no radiation).
Echocardiogram to assess for right ventricular strain/dysfunction, which would help risk-stratify this patient for possible PE and guide anticoagulation decisions. Safe in pregnancy.
ABG provides oxygenation and ventilation status in suspected PE in pregnancy, helping assess severity and guide management.
BNP/NT-proBNP assesses right heart strain, which is relevant in PE workup to stratify risk and guide treatment decisions.
BMP provides baseline renal function and electrolytes, important before initiating anticoagulation therapy in a pregnant patient with suspected PE.

CBC is warranted in a pregnant patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain to evaluate for anemia, thrombocytosis, or infection contributing to symptoms, and to establish baseline prior to potential anticoagulation.
Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) are essential to establish baseline clotting function in a pregnant patient with suspected PE before initiating anticoagulation therapy.
Lactate level helps assess for tissue hypoperfusion or hemodynamic compromise in the setting of possible pulmonary embolism, even with currently stable vitals.

Troponin is indicated to assess for right heart strain in suspected PE (acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain in a pregnant patient). It also helps risk-stratify the patient and has not been ordered yet according to the completed actions list.

In a pregnant patient with high clinical suspicion for PE (acute dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, CT-PA and Doppler ordered), LMWH (e.g., enoxaparin) is the preferred anticoagulant per guidelines. While imaging is pending, if clinical probability is high, empiric anticoagulation with LMWH should be initiated. LMWH is preferred over UFH and is safe in pregnancy.

Supportive IV fluid administration for hemodynamic support in suspected PE. While the patient is currently stable, maintaining adequate preload is important in PE management, particularly given pregnancy.

Consult interventional radiology proactively in case catheter-directed therapy becomes necessary, particularly relevant in a pregnant patient where systemic thrombolysis carries higher risk and CT-PA results are pending.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain in pregnancy, highly suggestive of pulmonary embolism. LMWH has already been given; transitioning to or continuing anticoagulation therapy is indicated for confirmed/high-suspicion PE in pregnancy. This is the next appropriate treatment step while CT-PA results are pending.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain in pregnancy, highly suspicious for pulmonary embolism. CT-PA and D-dimer have been ordered. Heparin (unfractionated) is the preferred anticoagulant in pregnancy when PE is confirmed or highly suspected, as it does not cross the placenta. Given the clinical picture and that LMWH was already given, transitioning to or supplementing with IV unfractionated heparin may be appropriate for ongoing anticoagulation management in this high-risk PE scenario.
